options.a: Stabilize the pelvis, limit movement, treat for shock
options.b: Compress and rock the iliac crests to confirm instability
options.c: Elevate the legs in shock position before splinting the pelvis
options.d: Apply a traction splint to the leg on the injured side

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated rocking or springing of the pelvis can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding; it is not used to confirm a fracture.
distractorExplanations.c: Raising the legs moves the fractured pelvis and delays stabilization; immobilize the pelvis first and limit movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Traction splints are contraindicated with pelvic fractures because the device pushes against the ischium and pelvis.

options.a: Remove it to reduce infection risk
options.b: Pull it out to control the bleeding
options.c: Stabilize it in place for transport
options.d: Cut it flush with the skin surface

distractorExplanations.a: Removal can release tamponade and cause severe bleeding.
distractorExplanations.b: The object may be tamponading bleeding; pulling it out worsens hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting it moves the object and can worsen tissue damage.

options.a: Low BP, distended neck veins, muffled heart tones
options.b: High BP, rapid pulse, and rapid shallow breathing
options.c: Low BP, slow pulse, and warm, dry skin
options.d: High BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing

distractorExplanations.a: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart tones are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade, not Cushing's triad.
distractorExplanations.b: Cushing's triad has a slow pulse (reflex bradycardia); hypertension with tachycardia suggests pain or sympathetic stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin describes neurogenic shock, not the hypertension of rising ICP.

options.a: Gently replace the organs, then cover with a moist dressing
options.b: Cover with moist sterile and occlusive dressings
options.c: Cover with dry sterile gauze secured by a tight wrap
options.d: Give small sips of water to treat the developing shock

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing eviscerated organs risks further injury and contamination; reduction is a surgical task, so cover them in place.
distractorExplanations.c: Dry gauze adheres to and dries the bowel, and a tight wrap compresses the organs; use moist sterile plus occlusive dressing.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal injury patients are kept NPO because they may need surgery and oral fluids risk vomiting and aspiration.

options.a: Immediate (red)
options.b: Delayed (yellow)
options.c: Minor (green)
options.d: Expectant (black)

distractorExplanations.a: Immediate is for patients who begin breathing after repositioning or have RR over 30, delayed cap refill, or cannot follow commands.
distractorExplanations.b: Delayed is for patients who breathe, have adequate perfusion and mental status, but cannot walk.
distractorExplanations.c: Minor (green) is for the walking wounded, not an apneic patient.

options.a: Pack the part directly in ice to slow tissue death
options.b: Submerge the part in sterile saline in a sealed container
options.c: Control bleeding; bag the part and keep it cool
options.d: Bag the part first, then dress the bleeding stump

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact freezes and damages the tissue; the sealed bag is kept cool on ice or cold packs without touching ice.
distractorExplanations.b: Soaking waterlogs the tissue and hampers reattachment; the part is wrapped in a sterile dressing per protocol, not immersed.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrong sequence: life-threatening bleeding at the stump is controlled first; the part is handled after the patient is stable.

options.a: Signs/symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last intake, Events
options.b: Saturation, Airway, Medications, Pulse, Level of consciousness, ECG
options.c: Scene, Allergies, Mechanism, Pulse, Last meal, Exposure
options.d: Signs/symptoms, Assessment, Medications, Pertinent negatives, Last vitals, Events

distractorExplanations.d: Mixes in non-SAMPLE terms: A is Allergies, P is Past pertinent history, and L is Last oral intake, not last vitals.
distractorExplanations.b: This mixes vital signs and monitoring into a list that is not SAMPLE.
distractorExplanations.c: Scene and mechanism belong to scene size-up, not the SAMPLE history.

options.a: Scene hazards and number of patients
options.b: The characteristics of pain or a symptom
options.c: A patient's past medical history and allergies
options.d: Level of consciousness and orientation

distractorExplanations.c: Past history and allergies are gathered with the SAMPLE history; OPQRST profiles the chief complaint itself.
distractorExplanations.a: Scene hazards are part of scene size-up.
distractorExplanations.d: Mental status is assessed with AVPU or GCS.

options.a: Visible chest rise with each ventilation
options.b: A pulse oximeter reading that rises within seconds
options.c: Resistance felt in the bag as each breath is squeezed
options.d: Abdomen rising and falling with each ventilation

distractorExplanations.b: SpO2 lags behind ventilation by a minute or more and can mislead with poor perfusion or CO; chest rise is the immediate sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising bag resistance suggests airway obstruction, gastric distension, or poor lung compliance, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach (gastric insufflation) from excess volume or poor head position.

options.a: Place in recovery position and observe
options.b: Ventilate with a BVM; consider naloxone
options.c: Give naloxone and wait for it to restore breathing
options.d: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min

distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone takes minutes to work; slow, shallow breathing must be supported with BVM ventilation first rather than waiting.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather needs adequate spontaneous breathing; slow, shallow respirations require assisted BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.a: Slow, shallow breathing needs assisted ventilation, not observation.

options.a: Lower airway narrowing from asthma
options.b: Fluid in the alveoli from heart failure
options.c: A normal breath sound in young children
options.d: Partial obstruction of the upper airway

distractorExplanations.a: Lower airway narrowing produces wheezing, not stridor.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluid in the alveoli causes crackles (rales).
distractorExplanations.c: Stridor is never a normal breath sound.

options.a: It can push the tongue back and block the airway
options.b: It can worsen a cervical spine injury
options.c: It raises intracranial pressure
options.d: It is less effective than a jaw-thrust in adults

distractorExplanations.a: Head-tilt/chin-lift lifts the tongue off the posterior pharynx; the trauma concern is neck extension worsening a spinal injury.
distractorExplanations.d: The head-tilt/chin-lift is usually the more effective maneuver; it is avoided in trauma because of neck extension, not efficacy.
distractorExplanations.c: The concern is spinal movement, not intracranial pressure.

options.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning with saturated hemoglobin
options.b: Significant hypoxemia needing urgent care
options.c: Severe anemia with normal oxygen saturation
options.d: Peripheral vasodilation from a warm environment

distractorExplanations.a: CO poisoning typically does not cause cyanosis; skin color and pulse oximetry can look falsely normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Anemia causes pallor; cyanosis needs enough deoxygenated hemoglobin, so anemic patients may not look cyanotic at all.
distractorExplanations.d: Vasodilation causes flushed, red skin; the bluish color of cyanosis reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin from hypoxemia.

options.a: The asthma attack is resolving on its own
options.b: The nebulizer treatment has fully worked
options.c: Worsening obstruction and respiratory failure
options.d: Drowsiness as a side effect of nebulized albuterol

distractorExplanations.d: Albuterol causes tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety, not sedation; drowsiness with poor air movement means fatigue and failure.
distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with drowsiness and poor air movement means less air is moving, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: Real improvement brings better air movement and alertness, not drowsiness.

options.a: One breath every 5–6 seconds (10–12/min)
options.b: One breath every 1–2 seconds (30–60/min)
options.c: One breath every 10–12 seconds (5–6/min)
options.d: One breath every 3 seconds (20/min)

distractorExplanations.b: This rate hyperventilates, raising chest pressure and lowering cardiac output.
distractorExplanations.c: Five to six breaths per minute underventilates an adult.
distractorExplanations.d: Twenty breaths per minute is a pediatric-range rate and too fast for an adult with a pulse.

options.a: The patient is apneic and needs artificial ventilation
options.b: A COPD patient needs precise low-flow oxygen titration
options.c: A breathing patient needs high-concentration oxygen
options.d: A stable patient with SpO2 of 93% needs mild supplementation

distractorExplanations.b: Precise FiO2 titration is the job of a Venturi mask; a nonrebreather delivers high, non-adjustable concentrations.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild hypoxemia in a stable patient is usually titrated with a nasal cannula toward 94%; the NRB is for high-concentration needs.
distractorExplanations.a: Apnea requires positive-pressure ventilation.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-015.explanation: NRB delivers high FiO2 to spontaneously breathing patients; apneic patients need BVM/advanced airway support. The patient must also be able to tolerate the mask.

options.a: About 1 inch (2.5 cm) for all adults
options.b: At least 3 inches (7.5 cm) or deeper
options.c: At least 2 inches (5 cm), full recoil
options.d: About one-half of the chest's depth

distractorExplanations.a: One inch is too shallow to circulate blood in an adult.
distractorExplanations.b: Compressions deeper than about 2.4 inches (6 cm) raise the risk of injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Adult depth is 2 to 2.4 inches; fractions of chest depth are used for infants and children, and one-half is too deep.

options.a: Check a pulse for a full minute first
options.b: Reanalyze the rhythm immediately after
options.c: Check for a carotid pulse for up to 10 seconds
options.d: Resume CPR for 2 minutes, then reanalyze

distractorExplanations.c: A post-shock pulse check delays compressions; resume CPR immediately and check rhythm and pulse at the 2-minute analysis.
distractorExplanations.a: Long pulse checks interrupt compressions.
distractorExplanations.b: Immediate reanalysis delays CPR; resume compressions first.

options.a: Peripheral edema and jugular venous distention
options.b: Crackles in both lungs and pink frothy sputum
options.c: Unilateral calf swelling with tenderness and warmth
options.d: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea at night

distractorExplanations.b: Pulmonary edema signs point to left-sided failure backing up into the lungs, not systemic right-sided congestion.
distractorExplanations.c: One swollen, tender, warm calf suggests deep vein thrombosis, not the bilateral dependent edema of right heart failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Orthopnea and PND reflect pulmonary congestion from left-sided failure rather than systemic venous congestion.

options.a: Dissolves established fibrin clots like fibrinolytics in the field
options.b: Inhibits platelet aggregation and may reduce clot progression
options.c: Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain quickly
options.d: Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose

distractorExplanations.c: Coronary vasodilation is the action of nitroglycerin; aspirin is given as an antiplatelet agent.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-dose (162–324 mg) aspirin is given for its antiplatelet effect, not analgesia; pain relief comes from nitro or opioids.
distractorExplanations.a: EMTs do not give field fibrinolytics as aspirin’s role.

options.a: Assume death since no pulse is palpable
options.b: Defibrillate with pads over the driveline
options.c: Follow local VAD protocols; call the VAD team
options.d: Disconnect the device power to reset its alarms

distractorExplanations.d: Disconnecting power stops the pump; VAD controllers and batteries stay connected and troubleshooting follows the VAD team.
distractorExplanations.a: VAD patients often lack a palpable pulse; that alone does not mean death.
distractorExplanations.b: Pads never go on the driveline or the device.

options.a: Treat airway, breathing, and circulation first
options.b: Complete a SAMPLE history before the hands-on exam
options.c: Splint every fracture before airway care
options.d: Transport only after a full secondary survey

distractorExplanations.b: SAMPLE history belongs to the secondary assessment; the primary survey addresses immediate life threats first.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway precedes orthopedic detail.
distractorExplanations.d: Load-and-go may interrupt full secondary survey.

options.a: Elevation and pressure-point compression
options.b: A loose pressure dressing and shock position
options.c: Direct pressure and a tourniquet
options.d: Tourniquet only after 10 minutes of pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for life-threatening bleeding; use direct pressure, then a tourniquet.
distractorExplanations.b: A loose dressing does not stop arterial flow, and Trendelenburg positioning is not a hemorrhage control method.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying a tourniquet for a fixed period wastes blood; apply it as soon as pressure fails or the bleed is clearly massive.

options.a: Blocking beta-2 receptors so the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes
options.b: Stimulating beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
options.c: Reducing airway inflammation over the next several hours
options.d: Thinning mucus so it can be coughed up more easily

distractorExplanations.a: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist (it stimulates the receptor); blocking beta-2 receptors would cause bronchoconstriction.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow anti-inflammatory action describes corticosteroids.
distractorExplanations.d: Mucolytics thin secretions; albuterol is a bronchodilator.

options.a: Right diagnosis, protocol, medical director, and destination
options.b: Right patient, drug, dose, route, and time, then document
options.c: Right vehicle, crew, radio channel, and destination
options.d: Right expiration date, lot number, packaging, and storage

distractorExplanations.a: Protocols and medical direction authorize a drug, but they are not the patient-safety rights checked at each administration.
distractorExplanations.d: Expiration is a supporting check; lot number and packaging are not among the core rights of patient, drug, dose, route, and time.
distractorExplanations.c: These are operational details, not medication rights.

options.a: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle to relieve wheezing
options.b: Constricting vessels to raise pressure and cut swelling
options.c: Slowing the heart rate so the ventricles fill better
options.d: Blocking histamine receptors to stop the hives and itching

distractorExplanations.d: Histamine blockade is the action of antihistamines such as diphenhydramine; epinephrine acts on adrenergic receptors.
distractorExplanations.a: Bronchodilation is a beta-2 effect of epinephrine.
distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine increases heart rate (beta-1); it does not slow it.

options.a: Start the primary survey on the most injured patient
options.b: Size up the scene for hazards and ensure scene safety
options.c: Request additional units before leaving the ambulance
options.d: Determine the mechanism of injury from bystanders

distractorExplanations.a: The primary survey comes after the scene is confirmed safe.
distractorExplanations.c: Requesting resources is part of size-up, but hazards and safety come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Mechanism of injury is assessed during size-up, after safety is addressed.

options.a: 0.04 mg sublingual, repeated every minute
options.b: 0.4 mg sublingual, repeated every 15 minutes
options.c: 0.4 mg sublingual, repeated every 5 minutes
options.d: 40 mg intramuscular in the deltoid

distractorExplanations.b: The repeat interval for SL nitroglycerin is 3–5 minutes; 15 minutes is the recheck interval after oral glucose.
distractorExplanations.a: 0.04 mg is a tenfold underdose, and one-minute repeats would not allow blood pressure reassessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin is not given intramuscularly by EMS.

options.a: Begin CPR and apply an AED as soon as possible
options.b: Give rescue breaths only, one every 6 seconds
options.c: Check a carotid pulse again for a full minute first
options.d: Check blood glucose before starting CPR

distractorExplanations.b: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient with a pulse and inadequate breathing; a pulseless patient needs compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds; prolonged checks delay compressions in a confirmed cardiac arrest.
distractorExplanations.d: Glucose checks delay CPR.

options.a: Clear the patient, shock, then check a pulse
options.b: Resume CPR, then shock at the end of 2 minutes
options.c: Clear the patient, shock, then resume CPR
options.d: Place pads over a medication patch

distractorExplanations.a: After the shock, CPR resumes immediately for 2 minutes; the pulse and rhythm check waits for the next analysis.
distractorExplanations.b: An advised shock is delivered promptly; delaying it lowers the chance of terminating VF or pulseless VT.
distractorExplanations.d: Remove medication patches and wipe the skin; shocking through a patch can cause burns and block current.

options.a: Blocks opioid receptors and displaces the opioid
options.b: Stimulates beta-2 receptors to open the airways
options.c: Reverses benzodiazepines at the GABA receptor
options.d: Raises blood glucose by releasing liver glycogen

distractorExplanations.b: Beta-2 stimulation describes albuterol, not naloxone.
distractorExplanations.c: Benzodiazepine reversal is flumazenil, which is not an AEMT medication.
distractorExplanations.d: Releasing liver glycogen is how glucagon works.

options.a: Recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or hypotension
options.b: Chest pain lasting more than 5 minutes
options.c: A systolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or higher
options.d: The patient already took aspirin today

distractorExplanations.c: Nitroglycerin is withheld when systolic BP is below about 90–100 mm Hg; 110 or higher is an acceptable pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Ongoing chest pain is the indication, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.d: Prior aspirin does not prevent nitroglycerin use.

options.a: 1 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration as a rapid IV push
options.b: 0.3–0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration into the lateral thigh
options.c: 3–5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration under the tongue
options.d: 0.03 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration into the deltoid muscle

distractorExplanations.d: That is a tenfold underdose using the IV-strength concentration; IM anaphylaxis dosing is 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL.
distractorExplanations.a: 1 mg IV push of 0.1 mg/mL is the cardiac-arrest dose, not anaphylaxis care with a pulse.
distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine is not given sublingually, and 3–5 mg is a dangerous overdose.

options.a: Asystole after two minutes of CPR
options.b: A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 readings
options.c: Fixed, dilated pupils after CPR
options.d: A palpable pulse after arrest care

distractorExplanations.b: ROSC typically causes an abrupt rise in ETCO2; a sudden drop suggests worsening perfusion or a displaced airway.
distractorExplanations.a: Asystole means there is no circulation.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed, dilated pupils suggest poor brain perfusion, not ROSC.

options.a: Possible acute coronary syndrome
options.b: Musculoskeletal strain of the chest wall
options.c: A panic or anxiety attack
options.d: Acid reflux from a recent meal

distractorExplanations.b: Radiating pressure is a classic ischemic pattern; ACS must be assumed first rather than attributing it to muscle strain.
distractorExplanations.c: Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion after ACS is ruled out.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflux can mimic ACS, but radiation to the arm or jaw must be treated as cardiac.

options.a: Oral glucose paste placed between cheek and gum
options.b: IM glucagon first, saving IV dextrose for a failed response
options.c: IV dextrose (for example D10 or D50) per protocol
options.d: Oxygen only, then recheck glucose in 15 minutes

distractorExplanations.b: Glucagon is the fallback when IV access fails; with a patent IV, dextrose acts faster and does not depend on liver glycogen.
distractorExplanations.a: Oral glucose needs an intact gag reflex and the ability to swallow; this patient is unresponsive.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen does not treat hypoglycemia, and waiting risks brain injury.

options.a: The patient has no liver glycogen stores at all
options.b: The patient is alert and able to drink juice safely
options.c: IV dextrose is available and a line is already running
options.d: IV access cannot be obtained

distractorExplanations.c: With a running IV, dextrose is preferred because it acts faster; glucagon is the fallback when IV access is not possible.
distractorExplanations.a: Without glycogen stores, glucagon has little or no effect.
distractorExplanations.b: An alert patient who can swallow should get oral glucose or food.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-015.explanation: Glucagon (IM or intranasal) releases stored liver glycogen as glucose. It is the fallback when IV dextrose is not possible. It works poorly when glycogen is depleted, for example in chronic alcoholism or malnutrition. In that case it is given IM or intranasally.
